unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Suncrest Olive Estate is a private limited company in Country X producing gourmet olive oil for export. It sells 400,000 bottles a year at $9 each, earning $3.6 million, and 60% of sales (240,000 bottles) go to buyers in Country W. The Country X dollar has appreciated by 12% against the Country W currency, so Suncrest's bottles now cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08 each unless it cuts prices.

Managing Director Lena Ortiz must set the June price list before orders for the next season close. Option A is to cut the Country W price to $8.10 a bottle, taking 10% off, to keep order volumes steady. Option B is to hold the $9 price and accept that Country W orders may fall sharply, shifting marketing towards domestic supermarkets instead.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so a currency buys more foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of a currency
Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% appreciation on Suncrest Olive Estate.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes Suncrest's oil more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. Each $9 bottle now costs Country W customers the equivalent of $10.08, so demand for the 240,000 bottles a year they buy may fall [app]. Second, appreciation weakens Suncrest's competitiveness against rival suppliers [k]. Country W supermarkets may switch to locally bottled olive oil instead, so Suncrest risks losing listings and part of its $3.6 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad
Appreciation reduces export competitiveness versus foreign rivals
application_max_2: Reference to $10.08 equivalent / 12% / $9 price
Reference to Country W 240,000 bottles / $3.6 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Suncrest Olive Estate might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the price by 10% reduces the revenue earned on every Country W bottle [k]. At $8.10 instead of $9, Suncrest loses 90 cents on each of its 240,000 Country W bottles, which is $216,000 a year less export revenue [app]. If volumes do not rise enough to replace this, profit falls and less money is available to reinvest in groves and bottling lines [an]. Second, a lower export price can trigger a price war with Country W rivals [k]. Rival producers may match the $8.10 offer to keep their supermarket listings, so Suncrest gains little extra shelf space [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across a market that takes 60% of sales, making the business less able to absorb future cost rises [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue per unit
Lower prices risk competitor price matching / price war
application_max_2: Reference to $8.10 vs $9 / 90 cents x 240,000 = $216,000
Reference to Country W / 60% of sales / supermarket listings
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to reduced profit and less funds for reinvestment
Chain from rival price matching to no extra volume and permanently lower margins

questions.question_text: Do you think Suncrest Olive Estate should cut the Country W price to $8.10 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the Country W price by 10% to $8.10 to hold order volumes steady [k]. This keeps Suncrest competitive now that its bottles cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08, helping to protect the 240,000-bottle order book that supplies 60% of its $3.6 million revenue [app]. Retaining shelf space prevents listings being lost to local Country W rivals, which would be hard and expensive to win back [an]. However, Option B holds the $9 price [k]. Refusing to discount protects the 90-cent margin on each bottle, so Suncrest avoids the $216,000 annual revenue loss built into Option A and keeps strong cash flow for the supermarkets [app]. The danger is that orders fall sharply as the 12% appreciation pushes Country W buyers towards cheaper local oil [an]. Overall, I think Suncrest should choose Option A [eval] because the appreciation was caused by currency markets rather than by Suncrest, and volume and shelf presence in Country W matter more than the margin; it can review the $8.10 price each season and raise it if the dollar weakens [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut price by 10% to $8.10 to defend volume
Option B: hold $9 and protect margin
application_max_2: Reference to $10.08 equivalent / 12% appreciation / 10% price cut
Reference to 240,000 bottles / 60% of sales / $3.6 million revenue / $216,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained competitiveness and protected Country W shelf space
Chain from holding price to preserved margin but risk of order losses to local rivals
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($8.10 vs $9, $216,000, 240,000 bottles)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Foxglove Denim Co is a private limited company in Country X weaving denim at its Glendale mill. It imports 30 tonnes of raw cotton a month from Country Z at $4,000 per tonne, costing $120,000 a month. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 15% against the Country Z currency, pushing the cotton price to $4,600 per tonne or $138,000 a month.

Managing Director Pavel Dvorak must decide on pricing by 1 August. Option A is to raise the wholesale price of jeans from $45 to $48 to protect profit margins, passing the $18,000 monthly increase to retailers. Option B is to keep prices at $45 and absorb the extra $216,000 a year, hoping cotton costs fall back or export sales to Country Z grow. 40% of Foxglove's jeans are exported.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so the currency buys less foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of a currency
Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 15% depreciation on Foxglove Denim Co.
questions.model_answer: First, depreciation raises the cost of imported cotton [k]. Cotton now costs $4,600 per tonne, so the monthly bill has jumped from $120,000 to $138,000, an extra $18,000 a month [app]. Second, depreciation makes Foxglove's jeans cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. With 40% of jeans exported to Country Z, the finished garments cost Country Z retailers fewer Country Z units, so export orders may rise and partly offset the higher cotton bill [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports
Depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad
application_max_2: Reference to $4,600 per tonne / $138,000 vs $120,000 / $18,000
Reference to 40% exported to Country Z

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Foxglove Denim Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, absorbing the increase squeezes profit margins on every pair of jeans [k]. The extra $216,000 a year must come out of the margin on jeans sold at $45, leaving less for repairs, machinery or wages at the Glendale mill [app]. Lower retained profit means less money available for future investment, such as replacing weaving looms, which weakens competitiveness [an]. Second, Foxglove cannot know when cotton costs will fall back [k]. If the Country X dollar keeps depreciating beyond 15%, the $138,000 monthly cotton bill could rise further, so a fixed $45 price leaves the firm exposed to open-ended cost growth [app]. Continued absorption would eventually push certain lines into loss-making months, forcing emergency price changes or borrowing [an].

knowledge_max_2: Absorbing costs squeezes profit margins
Currency costs may keep rising / future is uncertain
application_max_2: Reference to $216,000 a year / $138,000 monthly / $45 price
Reference to Glendale mill / further depreciation beyond 15%
analysis_max_2: Chain from absorbed costs to lower retained profit to weaker investment capacity
Chain from ongoing depreciation to open-ended cost growth to losses and forced price changes

questions.question_text: Do you think Foxglove Denim Co should raise its wholesale jean price from $45 to $48 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises the price by $3 to $48, passing the $18,000 monthly cotton increase on to retailers [k]. This restores margins without raising Foxglove's costs, which matters because depreciation lifted its bill from $120,000 to $138,000 a month [app]. Protecting $216,000 a year of margin lets Foxglove keep upgrading the Glendale mill and keeps its export pricing stable in Country Z terms [an]. However, Option B keeps prices at $45 [k]. Holding price may retain retailer loyalty and sales volume at home, and with 40% of jeans exported, stronger export volumes could offset the $216,000 absorbed [app]. The risk is that cotton costs keep rising if the dollar weakens further, so $45 may become unsustainable [an]. Overall, I think Foxglove should choose Option A [eval] because a $3 rise is only about 6.7% on a wholesale price and is caused by an external currency movement, so retailers are likely to accept it rather than lose supply; it should review the price each season in case cotton costs fall back [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: pass on cost via $3 rise to $48
Option B: hold $45 to protect loyalty and volume
application_max_2: Reference to $18,000 monthly increase / $216,000 a year / $45 to $48
Reference to 40% exports to Country Z / $120,000 to $138,000
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to restored margin to sustained investment
Chain from held price to volume retention but open-ended cost exposure
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($45 vs $48, $216,000, 40%)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ridgemont Electronics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling smartphone accessories at its Darnwell factory, employing 85 workers on two production lines. It imports circuit boards from Country W, paying €90,000 a month under a rolling supply agreement. The exchange rate has moved from $1.30 per euro to $1.45 per euro, so the dollar now buys fewer euros than six months ago.

Finance Director Mark Delgado must decide before the October supply contract is signed. Option A is to switch to a Country X circuit board supplier charging $135,000 a month, invoiced in dollars, with a 12-month fixed price. Option B is to keep importing from Country W at the current $130,500 a month and hope the rate swings back, accepting the uncertainty.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of the monthly €90,000 payment before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Before: €90,000 x $1.30 = $117,000. After: €90,000 x $1.45 = $130,500. The depreciation raises the monthly cost by $13,500 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Ridgemont Electronics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, the depreciation of the dollar raises the cost of imported circuit boards [k]. The monthly bill has increased from $117,000 to $130,500, an extra $13,500 a month that Ridgemont must absorb or pass on to customers [app]. Second, the movement reduces the reliability of Ridgemont's cost planning [k]. If the rate moves beyond $1.45 per euro, the $130,500 monthly import cost rises further, so the firm cannot confidently fix prices in its October supply contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker dollar makes imports dearer
Rate uncertainty makes cost planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to October supply contract / $130,500 vs $135,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ridgemont Electronics Ltd might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, the import cost is unpredictable month to month [k]. If the dollar weakens past $1.45 per euro, the €90,000 payment will exceed the current $130,500 and could approach the $135,000 charged by the Country X supplier [app]. Open-ended cost growth makes it hard to quote firm prices to customers, risking lost orders [an]. Second, continued importing keeps Ridgemont dependent on one foreign supplier and its lead times [k]. Any delay or disruption at the Country W factory would halt the Darnwell line that employs 85 workers [app]. A line stoppage would push up costs and damage reputation with accessory customers [an].

knowledge_max_2: Import costs can keep rising beyond current levels
Single foreign supplier creates dependency and lead-time risk
application_max_2: Reference to $1.45 per euro / $130,500 vs $135,000
Reference to Darnwell factory / 85 workers / October supply contract
analysis_max_2: Chain from further depreciation to import cost above $135,000 to eroded margin and lost orders
Chain from single-source dependency to line stoppage to costs and reputation damage

questions.question_text: Do you think Ridgemont Electronics Ltd should switch to the Country X supplier (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A switches to a local supplier charging $135,000 a month with a 12-month fixed price in dollars [k]. For roughly $4,500 a month more than the current $130,500, Ridgemont buys certainty: its October supply contract can be priced firmly and its 85 Darnwell workers face no supply interruption [app]. Locking $135,000 removes the risk that the dollar weakens to $1.50 per euro, at which point €90,000 would cost $135,000 anyway [an]. However, Option B keeps the lower import price [k]. If the rate swings back towards $1.30 per euro, the import bill returns to $117,000, saving Ridgemont $13,500 a month, or $162,000 a year, against the fixed contract [app]. The saving is not guaranteed and costs remain unpredictable in the meantime [an]. Overall, I think Ridgemont should choose Option A [eval] because fixed costs remove the guesswork from the October contract and a domestic supplier also shortens lead times; it can revisit the decision when the 12-month contract expires [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: fixed-price local supplier at $135,000
Option B: keep cheaper import at $130,500 / $117,000 if rate returns to $1.30
application_max_2: Reference to €90,000 / October supply contract / 12-month fixed price
Reference to $130,500 vs $135,000 / Darnwell / 85 workers
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed price to firm October pricing and no supply interruption
Chain from swinging rate to possible $162,000 annual saving forgone
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($135,000 vs $130,500, $1.30/$1.45)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Cider Co is a private limited company in Country X's northern vale pressing craft cider from 300 tonnes of apples a year. Half of its 150,000 cases a year are exported to Country W at €20 a case, invoiced in euros. The exchange rate has moved from $1.45 per euro to $1.30 per euro, so the dollar buys more euros than before.

Owner Gareth Rowe must set the export price list for January. Option A is to cut the Country W price by 10% to €18 a case to defend volume of 75,000 cases a year. Option B is to hold €20 and accept orders falling to 60,000 cases, increasing focus on domestic sales through farm shops and supermarkets instead.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar value of the annual export payments before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Annual exports: 75,000 cases x €20 = €1,500,000. Before: €1,500,000 x $1.45 = $2,175,000. After: €1,500,000 x $1.30 = $1,950,000. The appreciation cuts dollar export revenue by $225,000 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Carrowmore Cider Co.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the dollar value of Carrowmore's euro export sales [k]. The same 75,000 cases at €20 now convert to $1,950,000 rather than $2,175,000, so dollar export revenue falls by $225,000 [app]. Second, the appreciation makes it harder to recover that revenue by raising the export price [k]. Lifting the €20 price to claw back the shortfall would make Country W buyers switch to cheaper local cider, so Gareth must plan marketing carefully [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation lowers the dollar value of euro receipts
Raising foreign prices to recover revenue weakens competitiveness
application_max_2: Reference to Country W buyers / €20 a case / local cider rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Carrowmore Cider Co might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, holding price means giving up export volume [k]. Orders fall from 75,000 to 60,000 cases, so euro export revenue drops from €1,500,000 to €1,200,000, a loss of €300,000 a year [app]. Lower export volume may leave cider stockpiled for the domestic market, forcing farm-gate discounting [an]. Second, Option B shrinks Carrowmore's presence in Country W [k]. Once listings are lost to Country W rivals, winning them back is expensive, and farm shops and supermarkets at home may not absorb the extra 15,000 cases [app]. Domestic sales growth could lag, leaving the pressing plant underused and unsold stock [an].

knowledge_max_2: Holding price loses export volume and revenue
Lost listings are hard to recover / domestic market may not absorb displaced volume
application_max_2: Reference to 60,000 vs 75,000 cases / €300,000 loss
Reference to farm shops and supermarkets / Hereford vale / 15,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower export volume to unsold stock and farm-gate discounting
Chain from lost listings to higher re-entry cost and underused capacity

questions.question_text: Do you think Carrowmore Cider Co should cut its Country W price to €18 a case (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the export price by 10% to €18 to defend the 75,000-case order book [k]. Keeping 75,000 cases at €18 raises €1,350,000, which converts to $1,755,000 at the new $1.30 rate, well ahead of the 60,000-case alternative, and it keeps Carrowmore's cider listed in Country W stores [app]. Volume and shelf presence protect the brand abroad and spread fixed costs over more cases [an]. However, Option B holds €20 [k]. Orders fall to 60,000 cases, worth €1,200,000 or $1,560,000, but the margin per case is higher and the firm avoids cheapening its craft brand in its main overseas market [app]. The danger is losing momentum at the moment domestic farm shops and supermarkets are being asked to absorb extra cases [an]. Overall, I think Carrowmore should choose Option A [eval] because keeping 75,000 cases in front of Country W shoppers protects long-term export relationships while the firm builds domestic sales; it can restore €20 once the rate improves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut price by 10% to €18
Option B: hold €20, export volume falls to 60,000 cases
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to defended volume and protected shelf space and brand
Chain from holding price to higher per-case margin but lost listings and domestic pressure
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures (€18 vs €20, 75,000 vs 60,000 cases)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wren & Willow Fashion is a private limited company running 6 womenswear shops across Country X, employing 34 full-time and part-time staff. It imports 4,000 winter coats a year from Country W at €40 a coat, invoiced in euros. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, cutting the dollar cost of each coat from $58 to $52.

Buying Director Ines Duarte must decide the winter range prices before the January sales planning meeting. Option A is to cut the ticket price of imported coats by $6 to boost footfall and market share across the 6 shops. Option B is to keep ticket prices unchanged and keep the extra $24,000 a year, 4,000 coats at $6, as profit to refurbish 2 shops.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a stronger currency on businesses that import goods.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods become cheaper in the home currency; importers can cut their selling prices or enjoy higher profit margins [2].

knowledge_max_2: Imports cost less in the home currency
Importers can cut prices or raise margins

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Wren & Willow Fashion.
questions.model_answer: First, each imported coat now costs $52 instead of $58, saving $6 [k]. On 4,000 winter coats a year the total saving is $24,000, which can fund refurbishment or wage rises [app]. Second, cheaper coats let Wren & Willow compete on price without cutting its margin [k]. Passing on the $6 would keep relative value attractive to Country X shoppers while protecting the mark-up the shops need to pay 34 staff for 6 stores [app].

knowledge_max_2: Cheaper import costs in home currency
Scope to cut retail prices or boost margins
application_max_2: Reference to $52 vs $58 / $6 a coat / $24,000
Reference to 4,000 coats / 34 staff / 6 shops

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wren & Willow Fashion might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the ticket price sacrifices margin headroom [k]. Passing on the entire $6 import saving leaves no extra profit from the appreciation, so the $24,000 stays locked in lower prices rather than funding refurbishment of 2 shops [app]. If sales do not rise enough to offset the lower price, the business forgoes profit the currency change already delivered [an]. Second, price promotions can be matched by rival shops [k]. Competing Country X retailers importing from Country W will also face a $6 cost fall, so all may cut ticket prices together, leaving Wren & Willow with lower prices but little extra footfall [app]. Market-wide price cuts reduce revenue per coat and can squeeze cash flow during the crucial winter season [an].

knowledge_max_2: Passing on all the savings removes extra profit
Rivals can match price cuts
application_max_2: Reference to $6 / $24,000 / refurbish 2 shops
Reference to Country X retailers importing from Country W / winter season
analysis_max_2: Chain from full price pass-through to forgone profit if volume flat
Chain from rival price matching to market-wide margin squeeze and weaker cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think Wren & Willow Fashion should cut the ticket price of the imported coats by $6 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A passes the $6 saving straight to customers as lower ticket prices [k]. This makes the 4,000 imported coats noticeably better value, which should boost footfall across the 6 shops and lift market share before the winter peak [app]. Higher volume spreads fixed costs such as rent and wages over more coats and builds loyalty for the rest of the range [an]. However, Option B keeps ticket prices and banks the $24,000 [k]. The shops keep their margin, and the money could refurbish 2 of the 6 stores to improve customer experience without touching price [app]. The risk is that rivals cut prices first, leaving Wren & Willow uncompetitive on the high street despite the $6 saving being available [an]. Overall, I think Wren & Willow should choose Option A [eval] because the $6 saving was a currency windfall rather than genuine efficiency, and giving it back as value wins loyalty and share while margins stay at their pre-appreciation level [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut ticket prices by $6
Option B: hold prices and keep $24,000
application_max_2: Reference to $6 a coat / $24,000 / 4,000 coats
Reference to 6 shops / 2 shop refurbishment / 34 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from cut prices to footfall, market share and loyalty
Chain from held prices to funded refurbishment but risk of rivals undercutting
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($6, $24,000, 4,000 coats)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brannock Construction Ltd is a private limited company building 40 homes a year around Millbrook in Country X, mostly starter homes for young families. It imports structural steel and timber worth $1.2 million a year from Country W. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 8%, adding about $96,000 a year to material costs, and rates could move further either way.

Managing Director Rosa Ibanez must secure supplies before the spring building season begins on site. Option A is to sign with Country X steel and timber suppliers at 10% above import prices, totalling $1.32 million a year, but in stable dollars. Option B is to keep importing and raise homebuyers' prices to cover the extra $96,000 a year on top of site costs.

questions.question_text: State two ways a business can plan for exchange-rate fluctuations.
questions.model_answer: Monitor exchange-rate movements and adjust prices or sourcing in advance; agree contracts priced in the home currency or keep a contingency fund [2].

knowledge_max_2: Monitor rate movements and adjust prices or sourcing
Contract in home currency / keep contingency funds or reserves

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 8% depreciation on Brannock Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, the depreciation raises the cost of imported steel and timber [k]. The $1.2 million annual import bill now costs about $96,000 more, putting pressure on the margins of the 40 homes it builds a year [app]. Second, the depreciation squeezes Brannock's building economics unless home prices change [k]. Adding $96,000 across 40 homes means roughly $2,400 extra cost per home, which Brannock must absorb or recover through pricing [app].

knowledge_max_2: Depreciation raises the dollar cost of imports
Higher input costs squeeze margins / must recover through prices
application_max_2: Reference to $96,000 / $1.2 million / 8%
Reference to 40 homes / $2,400 per home / spring building season

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brannock Construction Ltd might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, domestic supplies cost $120,000 a year more than even the current import bill [k]. At $1.32 million against $1.2 million, Brannock pays a premium of $120,000, which is more than the $96,000 the depreciation added [app]. Higher material costs cut the margin on each of the 40 homes unless house prices rise [an]. Second, Country X steel and timber suppliers may not meet Brannock's volume or quality needs [k]. Millbrook builders all want local supplies at once, so lead times for domestic steel could run past the spring start, delaying the 40 homes [app]. Delays trigger penalty clauses in buyer contracts and raise site overhead, eroding the benefit of fixed prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Domestic suppliers charge more than imports
Local capacity and lead-time constraints
application_max_2: Reference to $1.32 million vs $1.2 million / $120,000 vs $96,000
Reference to 40 homes / spring building season / Millbrook
analysis_max_2: Chain from domestic premium to lower margin per home
Chain from local capacity limits to delays, penalties and overhead strain

questions.question_text: Do you think Brannock Construction Ltd should source steel and timber from Country X suppliers (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A locks in Country X supplies at $1.32 million a year with no exchange-rate risk [k]. Because Brannock sells homes on fixed prices, a further depreciation beyond 8% would otherwise destroy its margin on 40 homes, and $1.32 million gives complete cost certainty for the spring programme [app]. Certain costs make cash flow and profit planning reliable, protecting the business from open-ended import bills [an]. However, Option B keeps the cheaper import route [k]. The current $96,000 increase is smaller than Option A's $120,000 premium, and raising homebuyers' prices by about $2,400 a home might cover the extra while keeping imported materials [app]. Relying on homebuyers absorbing rises is risky if competing builders keep prices lower or the rate moves further against the dollar [an]. Overall, I think Brannock should choose Option A [eval] because its buyers have fixed-price contracts and cost certainty protects profit better than chasing a $24,000 saving that could vanish with one more rate move; it can return to imports if the dollar recovers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: domestic supplies at $1.32 million, fixed
Option B: keep imports and raise home prices by about $2,400
application_max_2: Reference to $120,000 vs $96,000 premium / 8%
Reference to 40 homes / $2,400 per home / spring building season
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed domestic costs to reliable planning and protected margins
Chain from homebuyer price rises to risk of losing sales to rivals
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures ($1.32 million vs $1.2 million, $96,000)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Thistledown Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in Country X importing 80 tonnes of green coffee a year from Country W at €2,800 a tonne, invoiced in euros, roasting them for independent cafe chains. The exchange rate has appreciated from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, cutting the annual bean bill from $324,800 to $291,200 and saving $33,600.

Founder Marta Kowal must choose how to buy next year's beans before the new season arrives. Option A is to sign a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne with the Country W supplier, locking costs regardless of rate movements. Option B is to keep buying monthly at spot rates and save even more if the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, a bill of $280,000.

questions.question_text: Define what is meant by a 'stronger currency'.
questions.model_answer: A stronger currency is one that has risen in value against other currencies, so it buys more foreign currency than before [2].

knowledge_max_2: Currency has risen in value
Buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Thistledown Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the annual green coffee bill [k]. At the new rate, 80 tonnes cost $291,200 rather than $324,800, saving $33,600 a year [app]. Second, the cheaper euros give Thistledown more room to compete and invest [k]. The $33,600 saving can be kept as extra profit or reinvested in roasting capacity without raising bean prices for cafe customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Import bill falls in the home currency
Savings can be kept as profit or reinvested
application_max_2: Reference to $291,200 vs $324,800 / $33,600 saving
Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / cafe customers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Thistledown Coffee Roasters might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the contract locks the cost even if the dollar keeps strengthening [k]. If the rate reaches $1.25 per euro, spot buyers would pay only $280,000 a year, so Thistledown would overpay by $11,200 against spot purchases [app]. Overpaying weakens the margin on every bag of beans and wastes funds that could finance growth [an]. Second, a 12-month fixed contract removes flexibility to switch suppliers [k]. If the Country W supplier's quality or reliability slips, Thistledown cannot easily move its 80 tonnes to a rival roaster without renegotiating, and it is exposed for a full year [app]. Being locked in limits negotiating power on quality, delivery and payment terms during the peak season [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed contract overpays if the currency keeps strengthening
Long contracts reduce flexibility to switch suppliers
application_max_2: Reference to 80 tonnes / €2,800 a tonne / Country W supplier

questions.model_answer: Option A signs a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne [k]. This locks the bill at $291,200 equivalent regardless of rate movements, so planning, pricing and cash flow are predictable for the whole year [app]. However, Option B keeps monthly spot buying [k]. If the dollar strengthens to $1.25 per euro, the annual bill falls to $280,000, saving $11,200 more than the contract, and buying monthly avoids being locked into one supplier [app]. The trade-off is exposure to sudden reversals, which could add tens of thousands of dollars of cost overnight [an]. Overall, I think Thistledown should choose Option A [eval] because predictable input costs protect the business's narrow roaster margins and support firm pricing with cafe customers; the $11,200 possible extra saving is not worth the risk of a reversal [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brinemare Fisheries is a private limited company fishing the cold waters off Country X's north coast, employing 60 crew and 12 factory staff. It exports 2,400 tonnes of frozen prawns a year, 70% of the catch to Country W supermarkets, at $4,000 a tonne, earning $9.6 million. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 10%, making its prawns cheaper in Country W shops.

Operations Director Sam Okoro must plan capacity for next year. Country W orders have risen by 25% to 3,000 tonnes, exceeding the 2,400-tonne freezing capacity. Option A is to invest $250,000 in a second blast freezer adding 800 tonnes of capacity. Option B is to hold output at 2,400 tonnes and quote new buyers higher prices and later delivery dates.

questions.question_text: Identify two types of business that benefit when a currency depreciates.
questions.model_answer: Exporting businesses benefit because their goods become cheaper abroad; home businesses competing with imports benefit because imports become dearer [2].

knowledge_max_2: Exporters benefit (goods cheaper abroad)
Home businesses competing with imports benefit (imports dearer)

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the depreciation for Brinemare Fisheries.
questions.model_answer: First, depreciation makes Brinemare's prawns cheaper for Country W supermarkets [k]. Orders have already risen by 25% to 3,000 tonnes, worth up to $12 million a year if the extra volume is met [app]. Second, the weaker dollar strengthens Brinemare's competitiveness against Country W prawn suppliers [k]. Country X product now undercuts rivals in Country W shops, so Brinemare can win longer-term listings rather than one-off orders on its 70% export share [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exports become cheaper abroad
Competitiveness against foreign rivals improves
application_max_2: Reference to orders up 25% to 3,000 tonnes / $4,000 a tonne / $12 million
Reference to 70% of catch to Country W supermarkets / $9.6 million

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Brinemare Fisheries might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the $250,000 investment is a heavy up-front cash outlay [k]. Brinemare earns $9.6 million a year, so $250,000 is about 2.6% of revenue, and it must be financed before the extra 800 tonnes can be handled [app]. If the money is borrowed, interest payments raise costs until the freezer pays back [an]. Second, the extra capacity depends on export demand lasting [k]. The 10% depreciation could be reversed, and a 25% order surge might fade; an 800-tonne freezer running half empty would burden Brinemare with labour and running costs [app]. Idle capacity would eat the profit from core 2,400 tonnes and could leave the firm overstretched [an].

knowledge_max_2: Large up-front investment must be financed
Demand surge may not last if the rate reverses
application_max_2: Reference to $250,000 / $9.6 million / 800 tonnes
Reference to 25% order rise / 10% depreciation / 2,400-tonne capacity

Chain from rate reversal to idle capacity and wasted running costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Brinemare Fisheries should invest in a second blast freezer (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A invests $250,000 in a second blast freezer adding 800 tonnes of capacity [k]. Demand has already risen 25% to 3,000 tonnes, so the investment would let Brinemare capture up to $12 million a year of prawn sales instead of turning customers away [app]. Extra volume spreads the fixed costs of 60 crew and the factory over more tonnes, improving profit per tonne [an]. However, Option B holds capacity at 2,400 tonnes and manages scarcity with higher prices and later delivery dates [k]. This protects margins on current sales without new finance, and higher prices could lift revenue per tonne from the fixed 2,400 tonnes [app]. The risk is that Country W buyers turned away now sign with rival suppliers and do not return when the capacity arrives [an]. Overall, I think Brinemare should choose Option A [eval] because refusing orders above capacity risks the permanent loss of Country W listings, while $250,000 is recoverable through the margin on extra tonnes; it can phase the investment over two fishing seasons to limit the cash risk [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Alderney Motors is a private limited company selling cars in Country X's capital city from a showroom near the ring road. It imports 18 cars a month from Country W at €26,000 each, invoiced in euros. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.45 to $1.30 per euro, so each car now costs $33,800 instead of $37,700, a saving of $3,900 per car or $842,400 a year.

Sales Director Ruth Adler must set showroom prices for the new plate month. Option A is to cut prices by $2,000 per car to attract buyers and increase monthly sales volume. Option B is to keep prices unchanged and keep the extra $70,200 a month in profit, using it to expand the service department instead.

questions.question_text: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods become cheaper in home-currency terms; foreign holidays and imported products become more affordable [2].

knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper
Foreign travel and imported products become more affordable

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Alderney Motors.
questions.model_answer: First, each imported car costs $3,900 less [k]. The monthly saving on 18 cars is $70,200, equal to $842,400 a year at the new rate [app]. Second, Alderney can choose how to use the saving [k]. A modest price cut of $2,000 a car would still leave most of the $3,900 saving intact while winning price-sensitive buyers from rival showrooms [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower import costs in home currency
Flexibility to cut prices or keep margin
application_max_2: Reference to $3,900 a car / $70,200 a month / $842,400
Reference to 18 cars / €26,000 / $33,800 vs $37,700

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Alderney Motors might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, the price cut gives back $36,000 a month of the $70,200 saving immediately [k]. The margin per car falls from $3,900 to $1,900, so Alderney keeps only half the windfall and volumes may not rise enough to compensate [app]. Weaker margins squeeze the cash available for staff, stock and the showroom, risking losses if sales stay flat [an]. Second, rival dealers will also see the appreciation lift their margins [k]. If they match a $2,000 cut, no showroom gains share, and Alderney's prices fall with no extra cars sold [app]. Market-wide discounting lowers revenue across the whole market and trains customers to wait for promotions rather than buy [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices sacrifices margin without guaranteed volume
Rivals likely to match the cut

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderney Motors should cut showroom prices by $2,000 per car (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts showroom prices by $2,000 a car to win buyers [k]. Because import costs fell to $33,800 from $37,700, this still leaves $1,900 of extra margin per car, and lower sticker prices should increase footfall and sales of the 18-car monthly quota [app]. More volume spreads overheads such as showroom staff and service bays, improving overall profit if sales respond [an]. However, Option B keeps prices unchanged and keeps the extra $70,200 a month [k]. Alderney banks a full $842,400 a year with zero risk to margin, which can expand the service department and deepen customer relationships after the sale [app]. The danger is that price-sensitive buyers drift to rivals who advertise lower prices, costing Alderney volume and long-term service work [an]. Overall, I think Alderney should choose Option B [eval] because the $70,200 monthly saving is certain while the volume gain from a $2,000 cut is not guaranteed; funding the service department strengthens the whole business, and selective promotions can target fence-sitters without a blanket cut [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Tarnmoor Medical Supplies is a private limited company in Country X making surgical gloves for hospitals and clinics. It exports 500,000 boxes a year to Country W, invoiced in euros, worth about €9 million a year, which is 70% of its revenue. The exchange rate has swung between $1.30 and $1.45 per euro over the last 12 months.

Managing Director Helen Varga must sign next year's supply deal with Country W distributors before the tender deadline. Option A is to fix the euro export price at €18 a box under a 12-month contract, with pricing built around $1.40 per euro. Option B is to re-quote prices every quarter at the spot rate, passing exchange-rate risk on to Country W buyers each time.

questions.question_text: Outline why many businesses prefer exchange rates to remain stable.
questions.model_answer: Stable rates let businesses plan and budget with confidence because the home-currency value of export receipts and import costs does not keep changing [2].

knowledge_max_2: Predictable planning and budgeting
No unexpected shifts in export revenue or import costs

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Tarnmoor Medical Supplies is worried about exchange-rate swings.
questions.model_answer: First, most of Tarnmoor's revenue comes from Country W exports [k]. With €9 million, 70% of revenue, invoiced in euros, a swing from $1.45 to $1.30 cuts export income from $13.05 million to $11.7 million, a loss of $1.35 million [app]. Second, the swing makes it hard to set prices and budgets [k]. Its costs in Country X, such as wages and materials, stay in dollars, so a $1.35 million revenue swing lands straight on profit, making the next year's plan unreliable [app].

knowledge_max_2: Most revenue is in foreign currency
Dollar costs against euro revenue create planning uncertainty
application_max_2: Reference to €9 million / 70% of revenue / $1.30 vs $1.45
Reference to 500,000 boxes / $13.05 million vs $11.7 million / $1.35 million swing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Tarnmoor Medical Supplies might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, quarterly re-quoting pushes risk onto Country W buyers but burdens them with uncertainty [k]. Buyers signing hospital supply contracts may switch to rivals offering fixed prices, especially as the rate swung a 15-cent range within a year [app]. Losing tendered contracts would damage Tarnmoor's market share precisely when it needs stable export income [an]. Second, re-quoting every quarter creates administrative work and disputes [k]. Four price lists a year, credit notes and contract changes would strain the small finance team, and buyers may query invoices whenever the $1.30 to $1.45 band bites [app]. Time spent renegotiating diverts management from production, and delayed or disputed payments would squeeze working capital while orders ship [an].

knowledge_max_2: Customers dislike unpredictable prices / risk of losing contracts
Admin burden and disputes from frequent re-quoting
application_max_2: Reference to quarterly re-quotes / Option B / Country W buyers
Reference to $1.30 to $1.45 / 500,000 boxes / hospital supply contracts
analysis_max_2: Chain from quarterly price changes to lost fixed-price tenders and export share
Chain from repeated renegotiation to admin strain and disputed payments

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarnmoor Medical Supplies should sign the 12-month fixed-price contract (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A fixes the euro export price at €18 a box under a 12-month contract built around $1.40 per euro [k]. Hospitals get one stable price all year, which protects Tarnmoor's 500,000-box order book and keeps its position against rivals in Country W [app]. Stable pricing encourages buyers to commit annual volumes rather than shop around every quarter, supporting reliable cash flow [an]. However, Option B re-quotes every quarter at the spot rate and pushes risk onto buyers [k]. If the dollar rises to $1.45, Tarnmoor would collect $13.05 million for the same €9 million, keeping $1.35 million more than at $1.30 [app]. But buyers may resist and demand fixed prices, so this theoretical gain may rarely be realised [an]. Overall, I think Tarnmoor should choose Option A [eval] because certainty wins long-term medical contracts and protects 70% of its revenue; $1.40 sits comfortably inside the $1.30-$1.45 band, so the deal is fair to both sides across a full year [eval].
